There are several ways to start, depending on how you like to work: In your browserBrowse, search, and publish nanopublications with Nanodash. Its templates mean you don't have to write RDF.On the command lineFetch, query, verify, and publish nanopublications with curl and the command-line tool. Follow the steps below.From codeUse a library for Java, Python, JavaScript, or Rust. There is a JavaScript example at the end of this page.With an AI agentAsk your coding agent to create, publish, and query nanopublications, using the nanopub Agent Skill. The steps below go from reading nanopublications to publishing your own. Steps 1 and 2 only need curl. Steps 3 and 4 use the command-line tool, which needs Java 21 or newer.

Every nanopublication has a resolvable URI. Ask for TriG and you get the RDF: curl -L -H "Accept: application/trig" \ https://w3id.org/np/RAlohixCBWPuGLSKA7mmR8k01EQvC_dRWwAU70kvvwKPo Open the same URI in a browser and you get a human-readable view in Nanodash. The examples page has more to try.
Published nanopublications are loaded into Nanopub Query instances. You can call ready-made queries through a REST API, or write your own SPARQL.

Each API endpoint runs a query that is itself published as a nanopublication. The endpoint URL is that nanopublication's ID plus the query name, and the placeholders in the query become URL parameters. This one is a full-text search: API=https://query.knowledgepixels.com/api curl -G $API/RAxdh5xkc6K6SMLY23yKu__zTWJPXeRFc0qgNNxkbOkpY/fulltext-search.csv \ --data-urlencode "query=Carabus granulatus" Nanopublications cannot be changed, so a new version is a new nanopublication that supersedes the old one. The announcement of Nano Session #29, for example, was edited several times. This query finds the latest version, starting from the first: API=https://query.knowledgepixels.com/api curl -G $API/RAiRsB2YywxjsBMkVRTREJBooXhf2ZOHoUs5lxciEl37I/get-latest-version-of-np.csv \ --data-urlencode "np=https://w3id.org/np/RAgITiAZA5yLltVB07D47Oo-kKVHOemwAkXnCq_ZYJtME" latest,date https://w3id.org/np/RAiODd0jLYxpvX3EHNpJfJr3mtcHgAo-QmYWoNYRqHvE0,2026-03-17T19:04:07.326Z The .csv suffix selects the result format, and .json works too. To see exactly what an endpoint does, fetch its definition like any other nanopublication: curl -L -H "Accept: application/trig" \ https://w3id.org/np/RAiRsB2YywxjsBMkVRTREJBooXhf2ZOHoUs5lxciEl37I Its assertion contains the SPARQL query, where the placeholder ?_np_iri becomes the np parameter. Because the definition is immutable too, an endpoint URL always runs the same query. This query lists all available ones.

The SPARQL endpoints cover all nanopublications. These are the five most recent ones: curl -G https://query.knowledgepixels.com/repo/full \ -H "Accept: text/csv" \ --data-urlencode 'query= PREFIX npa: <http://purl.org/nanopub/admin/> PREFIX dct: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> SELECT ?np ?label ?date WHERE { GRAPH npa:graph { ?np dct:created ?date ; rdfs:label ?label . } } ORDER BY DESC(?date) LIMIT 5' The npa:graph graph holds metadata that the query service adds for each nanopublication, such as its label, its date, and the public key it was validly signed with. This query finds all nanopublications whose assertion mentions the beetle species, leaving out the ones that their authors retracted or superseded with a new version: curl -G https://query.knowledgepixels.com/repo/full \ -H "Accept: text/csv" \ --data-urlencode 'query= PREFIX np: <http://www.nanopub.org/nschema#> PREFIX npa: <http://purl.org/nanopub/admin/> PREFIX npx: <http://purl.org/nanopub/x/> PREFIX dct: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> SELECT ?np ?label ?date WHERE { GRAPH ?assertion { ?s ?p <https://www.gbif.org/species/1036789> } GRAPH npa:graph { ?np np:hasAssertion ?assertion ; rdfs:label ?label ; dct:created ?date ; npa:hasValidSignatureForPublicKey ?pubkey . FILTER NOT EXISTS { ?newer npx:invalidates ?np ; npa:hasValidSignatureForPublicKey ?pubkey . } } }' To experiment, use the SPARQL editor in your browser.

Download the command-line tool of nanopub-java from Maven Central: V=$(curl -s https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/org/nanopub/nanopub/maven-metadata.xml \ | sed -n 's:.*<release>\(.*\)</release>.*:\1:p') curl -L -o nanopub.jar \ https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/org/nanopub/nanopub/$V/nanopub-$V-jar-with-dependencies.jar alias np='java -jar nanopub.jar' Save the beetle nanopublication and check it: curl -sL -H "Accept: application/trig" -o beetle.trig \ https://w3id.org/np/RAlohixCBWPuGLSKA7mmR8k01EQvC_dRWwAU70kvvwKPo np check beetle.trig Summary: 1 trusty with signature; 1 nanopub with issues "Trusty with signature" means that the hash in the URI matches the content, and that the signature is valid. The issue is only a warning that the nanopublication was created more than an hour ago, which matters when you publish a new one (np check -v shows the details). Now change a single label and check again: sed 's/Linnaeus, 1758"/Linnaeus"/' beetle.trig > tampered.trig np check tampered.trig Looks like a trusty nanopub BUT VERIFICATION FAILED: https://w3id.org/np/RAlohixCBWPuGLSKA7mmR8k01EQvC_dRWwAU70kvvwKPo Summary: 1 valid (not trusty); 1 nanopub with issues

Create a key pair. It is written to ~/.nanopub/, and existing keys are never overwritten: np mkkeys Write a nanopublication. It uses a temporary URI, which signing replaces with the final, hash-based one: cat > hello.trig <<EOF @prefix this: <http://purl.org/nanopub/temp/np001/> . @prefix sub: <http://purl.org/nanopub/temp/np001/> . @prefix np: <http://www.nanopub.org/nschema#> . @prefix dct: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> . @prefix prov: <http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#> . @prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> . @prefix xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> . @prefix orcid: <https://orcid.org/> . @prefix wd: <http://www.wikidata.org/entity/> . @prefix wdt: <http://www.wikidata.org/prop/direct/> . sub:Head { this: a np:Nanopublication ; np:hasAssertion sub:assertion ; np:hasProvenance sub:provenance ; np:hasPublicationInfo sub:pubinfo . } sub:assertion { wd:Q148 wdt:P36 wd:Q956 . # China - capital - Beijing } sub:provenance { sub:assertion prov:wasAttributedTo orcid:0000-0002-1825-0097 . } sub:pubinfo { this: dct:created "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"^^xsd:dateTime ; dct:creator orcid:0000-0002-1825-0097 ; dct:license <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/> ; rdfs:label "The capital of China is Beijing" . } EOF Replace 0000-0002-1825-0097 with your own ORCID iD. This one belongs to Josiah Carberry, ORCID's fictional test researcher. Then sign the nanopublication and publish it to the test server: np sign -s https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1825-0097 -o hello.signed.trig hello.trig np publish -u https://test.registry.knowledgepixels.com/ hello.signed.trig grep '@prefix this:' hello.signed.trig The last line shows the trusty URI of your new nanopublication. publish may warn that no templates are declared. Templates only matter for how Nanodash displays and edits a nanopublication, so you can ignore this warning here. Two things to know before you publish on the live network, which is what publish does without -u: Nothing can be deleted. You can supersede a nanopublication with a new version, or retract it with np retract, but the original stays on the network. Your key has to be linked to you. A signature proves which key signed, not who owns the key. For your nanopublications to be attributed to your ORCID iD, you declare your key in an introduction nanopublication (example), which an already trusted user then endorses. Nanodash generates a key for you automatically, and shows you how to publish the introduction.

The same steps in JavaScript with nanopub-js (npm install @nanopub/nanopub-js): import { Nanopub, NanopubClient } from '@nanopub/nanopub-js'; import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs'; import { homedir } from 'node:os'; // Fetch and search const client = new NanopubClient(); console.log(await client.fetchNanopub( 'https://w3id.org/np/RAlohixCBWPuGLSKA7mmR8k01EQvC_dRWwAU70kvvwKPo')); for await (const row of client.findNanopubsWithText('Carabus granulatus')) { console.log(row.np, row.label); } // Run a ready-made query for await (const row of client.runQueryTemplate( 'RAiRsB2YywxjsBMkVRTREJBooXhf2ZOHoUs5lxciEl37I/get-latest-version-of-np', { np: 'https://w3id.org/np/RAgITiAZA5yLltVB07D47Oo-kKVHOemwAkXnCq_ZYJtME' }, )) { console.log(row.latest, row.date); } // Sign and publish to the test server const np = Nanopub.fromRdf(readFileSync('hello.trig', 'utf8'), 'trig', { privateKey: readFileSync(`${homedir()}/.nanopub/id_rsa`, 'utf8'), orcid: 'https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1825-0097', }); await np.sign(); const { uri } = await np.publish('https://test.registry.knowledgepixels.com/np/'); console.log(uri); There are also libraries for Python, Java, and Rust, listed under Tools.

This is an incomplete list of systems that use nanopublications. If you know of one that is missing, let us know. Knowledge Collaboratory: annotate biomedical claims, publish the annotations as nanopublications, and browse nanopublications. Data Stewardship Wizard: publish FAIR implementation profiles as nanopublications. RiverBench: a benchmark suite for RDF systems, where users publish their benchmark results as nanopublications. RDF Stream Taxonomy (RDF-STaX): a living literature review of RDF streaming, maintained as nanopublications. fairworkflows: a Python library for constructing, modifying, and publishing scientific workflows described with semantic technologies.
Nanopublications are published in a decentralized network of services and applications. All components are open source, and the core services run as multiple instances.

A client, such as Nanodash, a library, or the command-line tool, creates a nanopublication, signs it, and sends it to any Nanopub Registry. The registries replicate nanopublications among each other. Nanopub Query instances load the nanopublications from a registry into triple stores. They offer SPARQL endpoints over all nanopublications, as well as over subsets such as a single type, a single public key, or the last 30 days. They also offer a REST API whose queries are themselves published as nanopublications. Nanodash and other applications read through Nanopub Query and publish through the registries. Because nanopublications are immutable and identified by hashes, any copy can be checked against its URI, no matter which instance served it.

Nanopub Registry (instance, code) is the second-generation service for publishing and retrieving nanopublications in a decentralized fashion. Nanopub Query (instance, code) is the second-generation service to query nanopublications. It allows for decentrally querying the published nanopublications via a number of SPARQL endpoints covering different subsets and aspects of nanopublications. Nanodash (instance, code) is a general client and user interface for nanopublications. It allows for user-friendly browsing, querying, and publishing of nanopublications, but can also be used as an API and intermediary layer for other services to build upon. The legacy nanopub-server (instance, code) still holds the old (unsigned) nanopublications, but otherwise no longer has a function in the latest generation of the ecosystem.

Nanopub Monitor (instance, code) observes the services that run the core components of the ecosystem. Vodex (code) is a vocabulary index service, used to provide auto-complete on third-party vocabularies. nanopub-http (code) provides features of the nanopublication libraries over HTTP, most importantly signing and publishing.

RAlohixCBW links a species of ground beetle to a habitat type. RAjcIFuVe7 states a scientific claim as an AIDA sentence and links it to more specific claims. RACK9s48ZO expresses a testable hypothesis in developmental biology, together with a proposed test. RAV_-_t50g defines a scientific variable as a FAIR Digital Object (FDO), following the I-ADOPT framework.

RAsyWOaZ7W states how three papers cite a given paper, with typed citations (CiTO). RAkDzG4wAG highlights a passage of a scientific article and comments on it. RAbp6LX5SR states that the creator has read a particular paper. RACEKjxyGN declares that the creator participates in a conference.

The nanopublication ecosystem is described in nanopublications too: users and their keys, the templates for creating nanopublications, the queries behind the API, and retractions. RASg5YBHps introduces a user and declares the public key they sign their nanopublications with. RALC35Q-V7 defines a template, from which nanopublications like the AIDA sentence above are created. RATC_tCEzO defines a SPARQL query, which is then available as an API. RAVa2aRzyu declares the retraction of another nanopublication.
The Nanopublication Guidelines specify the minimal formal structure of a nanopublication, and the Nanopublication Schema defines its vocabulary in RDF. This page summarizes them.

A nanopublication is a set of RDF quads in four named graphs: The assertion graph holds the main content. The provenance graph says how the assertion came to be, and must refer to the assertion graph. The publication info graph has metadata about the nanopublication as a whole, such as its creator and creation time, and must refer to the nanopublication. The head graph ties the three together and identifies the nanopublication. This is a minimal nanopublication in TriG, the recommended syntax: @prefix : <http://example.org/pub1/> . @prefix ex: <http://example.org/> . @prefix np: <http://www.nanopub.org/nschema#> . @prefix prov: <http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#> . @prefix xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> . @prefix dct: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> . @prefix orcid: <https://orcid.org/> . :Head { : a np:Nanopublication . : np:hasAssertion :assertion . : np:hasProvenance :provenance . : np:hasPublicationInfo :pubinfo . } :assertion { ex:trastuzumab ex:is-indicated-for ex:breast-cancer . } :provenance { :assertion prov:wasDerivedFrom :experiment . :assertion prov:wasAttributedTo orcid:0000-0003-3934-0072 . } :pubinfo { : dct:creator orcid:0000-0003-0183-6910 . : dct:created "2020-07-10T10:20:22.382+02:00"^^xsd:dateTime . }

A nanopublication is well-formed if: every triple is in one of the four graphs, and every graph has a URI; the head graph contains exactly one rdf:type np:Nanopublication triple, which identifies the nanopublication URI; the head graph links the nanopublication to exactly one assertion, one provenance, and one publication info graph; the URIs of the nanopublication and its four graphs are all different; the provenance graph refers to the assertion graph at least once, and the publication info graph refers to the nanopublication at least once.

Nanopublications are immutable, and their identifiers make this checkable. The recommended way is a Trusty URI: a URI that ends in a cryptographic hash of the nanopublication's content, like RAlohixCBW... in this example. Anyone who has the content can recompute the hash and check that it matches. The URIs of the graphs and of other resources the nanopublication defines are derived from its URI, so they are fixed by the hash too.

In the current ecosystem, nanopublications are also signed. The publication info graph then contains the creator's public key and a signature, and the trusty URI is computed over the signed content. The quick start shows how to sign, verify, and publish nanopublications.

This documentation is itself a set of nanopublications. It is a resource maintained by the Nanopublication space; each chapter is a topic, and each block of text within a chapter is a paragraph. Every topic and every paragraph is a nanopublication of its own, signed by whoever wrote it, and the pages you are reading are assembled from them by a query. That makes the documentation a wiki: any member of the space can add a chapter, add a paragraph, revise or remove one, and the history of every change is preserved. Members of the Nanopublication space — at member tier or above — can add and edit. What they publish appears on the pages; what anyone else publishes about the same topics is stored on the network but not shown here. To become a contributor, ask an admin of the space for a role. You can also declare yourself an observer of the space in the meantime, which is a way of saying you are interested; it does not by itself let your edits show. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A chapter is about a thing, and it is identified by that thing's own URI: the chapter on templates is about the class of nanopublication templates, the chapter on spaces about the class of spaces. To add a chapter, use "add topic…" above the list of chapters, which opens the "Declaring a documentation topic" form: give the URI, a title, and this documentation as the collection it belongs to. A position, such as 210, places the chapter in the list, and a one-sentence description is shown there under its title. A chapter about something without a URI of its own — a tool, a way of working — gets one under this documentation's namespace, https://w3id.org/spaces/nanopub/r/docs/, and names what it covers with the form's "is about" field. The form has another field, "the described resource", in its publication-info section; enter the chapter's URI there too. It is what makes the chapter get a page of its own — without it the chapter is listed but cannot be opened. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

On a chapter's page, "add paragraph…" opens a form asking for a title, the text, and a position. The text can be plain, or simple HTML for emphasis, code and links. Keep a paragraph to one point; a chapter reads best as a series of short, titled blocks rather than a few long ones. The paragraph is published under your name and appears on the page as soon as the network has picked it up, usually within a minute. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Every paragraph has a page of its own: click its heading, or choose "open" from its menu. The page shows the paragraph's current text with its "edit…" and "remove…" entries, the examples linked to it, the paragraphs related to it, and its version history — every version anyone published, newest first, with the current one marked. Three things are done from there. "Add example…" links anything with a URI — a nanopublication, a page, a service address — as an example of what the paragraph describes, with a short note on what to look at. "Add related paragraph…" links it to a paragraph a reader should also see, possibly in another chapter; the link shows on both pages. And "restore this version…" in the history makes an earlier version current again, whoever published it. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Every paragraph has an "edit…" entry in its menu, whether you wrote it or someone else did. It opens the form with the current text; publishing makes a new version that keeps the paragraph's identity, and the page shows the newest version by any member. The earlier version is kept, listed in the paragraph's version history, and can be restored from there. So a correction to someone else's text is made the same way as to your own. Nothing needs the original author's key, and nothing is lost. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Paragraphs are ordered by their position, a short text such as 030 compared letter by letter. Positions in tens leave room: a paragraph to go between 030 and 040 gets 035. Paragraphs without a position come first, in title order, so give every paragraph one. A paragraph can be moved by editing its position, and a whole chapter renumbered the same way, one edit per paragraph. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Every paragraph has a "remove…" entry in its menu, open to any member, whoever wrote the paragraph. It publishes a new version that marks the paragraph as removed, with an optional reason. The paragraph then disappears from its chapter and from the chapter's paragraph count, and its own page shows a notice in place of the text. A removal is undone like any other change: the version history lists it, and "restore this version…" on an earlier row brings the text back. A whole chapter is removed the same way from the list of chapters, and restored by adding it again with the same URI. Retracting is still open to whoever published a version, but it withdraws only that version, and the one before it, if any, becomes current again. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Say what a thing is for before saying how it works. Use the vocabulary terms a reader will have to type, and explain the rest in words. Prefer one concrete example to a list of options. Where a fact depends on a version of a tool, say so, since these pages outlive releases. And when you are unsure whether something is still true, check it before writing it down — a wrong sentence here is read by everyone who comes after you. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash This page is a copy of the topic Documentation topic of the Nanopublication Docs. Each paragraph is a nanopublication. In Nanodash you also find their examples, related paragraphs, and version history, and members of the nanopub space can edit them there.
Things a space takes responsibility for: declaring them, namespaces and parts, who may do what, and shared definitions.

A maintained resource is something a space takes responsibility for and gives a page to: a vocabulary, a collection of documents, a set of documentation like this one, a systematic review, a shared template. The resource is identified by a URI; the space is what says who may work on it and what its page shows. Declaring one is a single nanopublication by an admin of the space: the resource's URI, a name, a description, the space that maintains it, and optionally a type and a namespace. From then on the resource has a page hosted within the space. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A resource can be typed to say what it is — an ontology, a concept scheme, a collection, a systematic review, an assertion template — and the type says which ready-made views suit its page, which the space then attaches: a vocabulary gets lists of its classes and terms and an action to release a version, for instance. A resource without a type is a plain page that its admins furnish with views of their choosing. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A resource may declare a namespace: a URI prefix, such as https://w3id.org/spaces/example/r/vocabulary/, under which the things belonging to it are minted. Anything with a URI under that prefix is a part of the resource, and gets a page of its own, hosted within the resource's page, showing what the network knows about it. A part's page is put together from the nanopublication that introduced it, which must have been published by a member of the space. Links to a part from anywhere on Nanodash lead to that page, so the namespace is also what makes a resource's terms, entries or paragraphs navigable rather than bare URIs. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Declaring a resource, attaching views to its page and choosing its presets are for admins and maintainers of the space. Contributing to its content — defining a term, adding an entry, writing a paragraph — is for the space's members, and the pages of collaboratively edited resources show what members have contributed. Observers and outsiders can read everything but their contributions, though stored on the network, are not shown. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A space can also list a template or a view as one of its maintained resources. The point is less to give it a page than to take charge of its versions: once the space maintains the template or view, the current version is the newest one published by any member of the space, rather than by whoever published the previous one. That is how a community keeps its shared tools current after their original author has moved on. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash This page is a copy of the topic Maintained resource of the Nanopublication Docs. Each paragraph is a nanopublication. In Nanodash you also find their examples, related paragraphs, and version history, and members of the nanopub space can edit them there.
documents.s: A resource as a shared definition

documents.t: What a nanopublication is: its four parts, its content-based identifier, its signature, and why it never changes once published.

A nanopublication is the smallest unit of publishable information: a few statements that together say one thing, packaged with who made them and where they come from. It is written as RDF, so both people and software can read it, and each one has its own web address. Anything can be the subject: a scientific claim, a definition of a term, a link between two things, an opinion, a piece of documentation like this paragraph. What matters is that each nanopublication makes one point and carries its own attribution. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Every nanopublication has four parts, called graphs. The assertion holds the actual content. The provenance says where that content comes from: who asserted it, what it was derived from. The publication info describes the nanopublication itself: when it was created, by whom, under which license, and its digital signature. The head is a short list that names the other three. In the RDF this looks like: this: a np:Nanopublication ; np:hasAssertion sub:assertion ; np:hasProvenance sub:provenance ; np:hasPublicationInfo sub:pubinfo . Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

The assertion is the content, and it can be any RDF. Most nanopublications keep it small — one to a handful of statements — because a nanopublication is meant to be about one thing. If two things need saying, they are better said in two nanopublications, each of which can then be referred to, revised or retracted on its own. Whatever a nanopublication introduces — a new term, a new resource, a new definition — is identified by a URI in the assertion, normally minted under the nanopublication's own address. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

The provenance part says where the assertion comes from. The two most common statements are prov:wasAttributedTo, naming the person or agent who made the assertion, and prov:wasDerivedFrom, pointing to a source such as a paper, a dataset, or another nanopublication. Provenance is about the content, not about the act of publishing: a nanopublication that copies a claim from a paper attributes the claim to the paper here, while the person who did the copying appears in the publication info as the creator. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

The publication info describes the nanopublication as an object. It usually holds the creation time (dct:created), the creator (dct:creator), a license (dct:license), and a short label (rdfs:label) that is shown wherever the nanopublication is listed. It also records which templates were used to make it, which lets it be reopened and revised in a form later. This is also where the digital signature lives, and where a nanopublication says what it introduces, describes, or supersedes. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A nanopublication's address ends in a code computed from its own content, such as RAGtlyskGNfHtX-dWRqUoSx6nPc0P0st6WII5zRpF9CUw. Such addresses are called trusty URIs. Because the code is derived from the content, the content cannot change without the address changing too, and anyone holding a copy can verify that it is the genuine one. The code always starts with RA and is 45 characters long. The full address is usually written as https://w3id.org/np/RA…, which resolves to the nanopublication on the network and can be opened in a browser. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A nanopublication is signed with a private key, and the signature is stored in the publication info together with the matching public key and the identity of the signer. The signature covers the whole content, so it proves that the nanopublication was made by the holder of that key and has not been altered since. Keys belong to people and to software agents. A person links a key to their identity by publishing an introduction nanopublication, and once the network has accepted that introduction, everything signed with the key counts as theirs. Signatures are what the network uses to decide whose word counts for what — which nanopublications a person may retract, which spaces they belong to, and so on. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Once published, a nanopublication cannot be edited, and it cannot be deleted from the network either. The address is tied to the content, and copies spread to several servers as soon as it is published. Instead of editing, one publishes a new version that supersedes the old one, and instead of deleting, one publishes a retraction. Both leave the original in place but tell every tool to treat it as outdated. This is what makes a nanopublication citable: what was cited stays exactly as it was, even after its author has moved on. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Nanopublications are published to a network of registries. It is enough to send a nanopublication to one of them; the others pick it up from their peers within minutes. Tools such as Nanodash and the command-line client do this for you. There is a separate test network for trying things out. Nanopublications published there do not reach the real network and are not counted by it, so it is the place for experiments and for a first attempt at something new. On the real network, publishing is final. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Every nanopublication can be opened directly by its address. Beyond that, the network keeps them searchable by their types, by who published them, by what they introduce, and by full text. Nanodash shows nanopublications in the context of the spaces, resources and people they belong to, and Nanopub Query offers the same data as an API for software. A nanopublication is easier to find, and more useful once found, when it carries a good label and a type — see the publication info — and when the things it introduces have labels of their own. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Subjects and objects in a nanopublication may be identified by http and https URIs, and also by content-addressed ipfs and ipns identifiers and by decentralized did and at identifiers. Predicates, and the addresses of the nanopublication and its four parts, must be http or https. Older tools accept only http and https everywhere, and some display the newer identifier kinds as plain text rather than as links. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Nanodash is the web application for reading, creating and publishing nanopublications; it is where the forms, spaces and pages described in this documentation live. The command-line client, nanopub-java, checks, signs, publishes and retracts nanopublications from a terminal, and is also the library behind Nanodash and the registry. Libraries exist for Python and JavaScript as well. Whichever tool is used, the result is the same kind of nanopublication, and one made with one tool can be opened and revised with another. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash This page is a copy of the topic Nanopublication of the Nanopublication Docs. Each paragraph is a nanopublication. In Nanodash you also find their examples, related paragraphs, and version history, and members of the nanopub space can edit them there.
A nanopublication that lists other nanopublications: size, chaining, and making one.

An index is a nanopublication whose content is a list of other nanopublications. It gives a set of nanopublications a single address and a single signature: a released version of a vocabulary, the outputs of a project, the evidence behind a review. Citing the index cites exactly that set, as it was when the index was made, whatever happens to its members afterwards. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

An index holds up to a thousand entries. A larger set is split into several indexes chained together, each appending to the previous, and an index can also include other indexes as sub-indexes, so a collection of any size has one top-level address. Tools follow the chain when they read the set. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

The command-line client builds an index from a list of nanopublication files or addresses, with a title, and signs it like any other nanopublication. A vocabulary's release action does the same from within Nanodash, collecting the currently approved terms. An index is updated by publishing a new one that supersedes it; the old index remains, still describing the set it described. In Nanodash you also find their examples, related paragraphs, and version history, and members of the nanopub space can edit them there.
Query templates in the grlc style: placeholders, parameters, result columns, testing and the rules for writing them.
Nanopublication SPARQL templates use an extended version of the grlc syntax. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Every query template names the repository it runs against, as the object of <https://w3id.org/kpxl/grlc/endpoint> in its assertion. The usual choice is the full repository, which holds every loaded nanopublication: <https://w3id.org/np/l/nanopub-query-1.1/repo/full> Other repositories are narrower and therefore faster: meta for nanopublication metadata, text for full-text search, last30d for recent nanopublications, and a per-type repository type/<hash> or per-key repository pubkey/<hash>. Two further repositories, spaces and trust, hold the server-side computed state of space membership and of the agent-to-key trust network; a query can reach them from another repository with a federated service clause. Always write the endpoint with the generic w3id.org/np/l/nanopub-query-1.1/ prefix rather than the host name of one instance. The prefix is rewritten to whichever instance answers the query, so a template naming a single host stops working as soon as that host does. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Nanopublication query templates use variable names starting with "_" to denote placeholders, following grlc syntax. Those that end in "_iri" like "?_resource_iri" are IRI placeholder; otherwise they are literal placeholders, like "?_name". The name of the API parameter is the variable name with the prefix and the type suffix removed: ?_resource_iri is filled by a parameter called resource, and ?_name by one called name. The underscores and the "_iri" never appear in the request. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Optional placeholders in nanopublication query templates also follow grlc syntax. Such optional placeholders, which don't necessarily need to be filled before running the query, start with two underscores instead of just one, e.g. "?__filter_iri" or "?__filtertext". Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Nanopublication query templates extend grlc syntax by supporting placeholders that can have more than one value. Those have the suffix of "_multi_iri" (for IRIs) or just "_multi" (for literals). Importantly, they only work if there is at least one occurrence of a "values" statement like "values ?_resource_multi_iri {}", which indicates where the values are filled in. These multi-value placeholders take 1 or more IRIs/literals. Every subquery scope needs its own values block. A block in the outer query does not reach into a subquery, and the mistake is silent: the subquery simply matches nothing and the query returns no rows rather than an error. Starting the name with two underscores instead of one makes a multi-value placeholder optional, as in ?__resource_multi_iri, which accepts zero or more values. With none given, the values block stays empty and the query still runs unconstrained. This is the only placeholder form that can both be tested in the query and be left unfilled. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A single-value placeholder is not a bound SPARQL variable. Its value is substituted into the query as text before the query is parsed, so by the time the query runs the placeholder is gone and only the value remains. The practical consequence is that bound(?_name) cannot be used: it becomes bound("some value"), which is not valid SPARQL. Guard a comparison with coalesce instead, which yields the fallback when the comparison cannot be evaluated: filter(coalesce(?date >= ?_startDate, false)) Multi-value placeholders behave differently: they are bound through their values block and are ordinary variables inside the query. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash
documents.s: Single placeholders are substituted as text

documents.t: A literal placeholder is substituted as an untyped string, so comparing one against a typed value such as dct:created silently matches nothing: an untyped string and an xsd:dateTime are not comparable in SPARQL. Cast the placeholder explicitly wherever it is compared: filter(?date >= xsd:dateTime(?_startDate)) The value passed by the caller must then be a full ISO 8601 date and time, for example 2026-03-01T00:00:00Z. A bare date such as 2026-03-01 makes the cast fail. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Three placeholder names are reserved and filled automatically from the browser session of whoever is looking at the view, with no form field shown: LOCALPUBKEY is the viewer's signing public key, CURRENTUSER their agent IRI, and SITEURL the address of the Nanodash instance. They let a view react to who is viewing it, for example by offering a "retract" action only on rows the viewer signed. Declare them as optional multi-value placeholders, each with its own empty values block in every scope where it is used: ?__LOCALPUBKEY_multi, ?__CURRENTUSER_multi_iri, ?__SITEURL_multi. A logged-out visitor has none of them, so the variable is simply unbound and every comparison must tolerate that. Wrap each one in coalesce, as in coalesce(str(?pubkey) = str(?__LOCALPUBKEY_multi), false), so the query still returns its rows instead of failing or dropping them. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A placeholder whose parameter name is context is filled automatically with the resource whose page the view is being shown on. Nothing needs to be declared beyond the placeholder itself. On a resource's own page that is the resource. On the page of one of its parts it is the owning resource, while the view's own target field receives the part; both arrive in the same request. This is what lets a query about one part still find the space that maintains it, without naming that space in the query. Declare it as an optional multi-value placeholder, ?__context_multi_iri, with its own values block in each scope. A federated service sub-select that uses only this placeholder shares no variable with the outer query and is therefore evaluated once, rather than once per result row. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Result columns that hold a URI can have a companion variable with a "_label" suffix to control how the value is displayed. The UI renders the label text as a clickable link to the URI. For example, a "?event" column paired with "?event_label" will display the label linked to the event URI. Without a label companion, the system renders URIs with its default formatting. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

To include a link to the source nanopub in query results, add "?np" and "?np_label" as the last two columns in the SELECT clause, in that order. Use ("^" as ?np_label) to display a short clickable caret symbol instead of the full nanopub URI. These should always be placed at the end of the column list. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

When concatenating literal values with a newline separator in group_concat, always escape existing backslashes and replace CR/LF sequences in the individual values first: replace(replace(?val, "\\\\", "\\\\\\\\"), "[\r\n]+", "\\\\n"). First escape existing backslashes (\\ → \\\\), then replace any sequence of CR/LF characters with the two-character escape \\n. This ensures values containing these characters can be safely split on newlines later. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

The "_label" naming convention extends to multi-value columns. For a "?things_multi_iri" column holding whitespace-separated URIs, use "?things_label_multi" as its label companion holding newline-separated labels (with the same escaping as for "_multi" literals). For example, "?authors_multi_iri" (whitespace-separated ORCIDs) paired with "?authors_label_multi" (newline-separated names) displays each author name linked to their URI. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A result column whose variable name ends in "_noheader" is still rendered, but with its header label blanked. When no remaining column has a visible header, the header row disappears altogether, which suits a view meant to read as a list rather than a table. The marker is stripped before the column name is interpreted, so type suffixes, "_label" companions and action mappings all keep matching the name without it. The companion columns themselves are left unmarked. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A result column whose variable name ends in "_group" is not shown as a column. Instead the table gets a heading row wherever that column's value changes from one row to the next, so the query's order by decides the groups and their order. Clicking a column header then sorts the rows within each group and leaves the groups in place. Give every row of a group exactly the same value, and make it read well on its own, since it becomes the heading. Nanodash supports this from version 5.17; older versions show the column as an ordinary one. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

When a query nanopublication is written by hand, the SPARQL sits inside a TriG string literal, and the TriG parser resolves backslash escapes before the SPARQL is ever seen. Every backslash meant for the SPARQL must therefore be doubled in the file. The one that catches people is the separator of group_concat. Written as a single backslash, separator="\n" becomes a real line break inside a quoted SPARQL string, which is not valid SPARQL. Written as separator="\\n" in the TriG, it reaches the query as the two characters that were intended. The safe way to produce the file is to build it from the raw query text with the backslashes doubled programmatically, then parse the result back and check that the round-tripped literal still contains the escape rather than a line break. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash
documents.s: Writing the SPARQL into the TriG

documents.t: A nanopublication cannot be changed once published, so a query whose SPARQL does not parse would be broken permanently: it could never run, and the only remedy would be publishing a corrected version. Since nanopub-java 1.94.0 both signing and publishing refuse such a nanopublication, reporting the parser's own error, and check reports it as an issue. This catches the doubled-backslash mistake at signing time rather than after publication. Where the parser stops at a character outside ASCII, the message names it, because these queries are more often broken by a character picked up from a word processor or a web page than by a mistyped keyword. A non-breaking space, for instance, is reported as Encountered: '160' (160). Older versions of the tool have no such check: they sign and publish the nanopublication, and only the query API rejects it afterwards. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A query template can be run before it is published. Encode the signed nanopublication in base64url and pass it as the _nanopub_trig parameter of an ordinary API call, together with the parameters the query expects. The service then answers using that nanopublication as if it had been published. The same parameter works on the OpenAPI page, which gives a form for the query's parameters and is the easier way to try several values. Testing this way matters because the checks made at signing time are about syntax only. A query that parses can still join nothing, return the wrong rows, or be too slow, and none of that is visible until it runs. Note also that a large query nanopublication makes the request too long for the w3id.org redirector, which answers with error 414. The query service itself accepts it, so send the same request to an instance's own address, such as https://query.knowledgepixels.com/api/…, rather than falling back to the bare repository, which skips the template's parameter handling. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash This page is a copy of the topic Nanopublication query template of the Nanopublication Docs. Each paragraph is a nanopublication. In Nanodash you also find their examples, related paragraphs, and version history, and members of the nanopub space can edit them there.
Templates that describe the shape of a nanopublication: statements, placeholders, resources, versions, settings, and fill modes.

A template is itself a nanopublication. It describes the shape of one part of some other nanopublication as a list of statements, with placeholders standing where the values are still to come. Nanodash turns a template into a form, and publishes the filled-in values in place of the placeholders. Because a template is an ordinary nanopublication, it is signed, versioned and citable like any other, and the nanopublications made from it record which template they came from. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

There is one kind of template for each part of a nanopublication that gets filled in: nt:AssertionTemplate for the assertion, nt:ProvenanceTemplate for the provenance, and nt:PubinfoTemplate for the publication info. All three are subclasses of nt:NanopubTemplate and work the same way. A publish form combines one assertion template, one provenance template, and any number of publication-info templates. The assertion template is the one you pick; it gives the form its name and normally brings sensible defaults for the other two. A template can additionally be typed nt:UnlistedTemplate. It is then no longer offered when creating new nanopublications but stays usable by its URI, so nanopublications already made from it can still be opened and updated. This is how a template is retired without breaking anything. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Templates are made with a template. Nanodash offers "Defining an assertion template" (and counterparts for provenance and publication-info templates), where you enter the statements and placeholders described below in a form and publish the result. A newly published template shows up in the template lists shortly afterwards, grouped under its tag. A template can also be written by hand as a nanopublication file and published with the command-line tools. The result is the same kind of nanopublication either way, so a hand-written template can later be reopened and revised in the form. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

The body of a template is its statements, each listed with nt:hasStatement and described by rdf:subject, rdf:predicate and rdf:object: sub:st1 rdf:subject sub:paragraph ; rdf:predicate schema:title ; rdf:object sub:title . Any of the three positions may be a fixed IRI, which then appears unchanged in every nanopublication made from the template, or a placeholder, which the user fills in. Fixed IRIs are usually given an rdfs:label in the template, so the form can show words rather than URIs. Where the order of statements matters, it is set with nt:statementOrder. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A statement typed nt:OptionalStatement may be left empty, and is then simply absent from the published nanopublication. One typed nt:RepeatableStatement can be filled more than once, which gives the form an "add another" control. A statement typed nt:GroupedStatement contains other statements, again listed with nt:hasStatement, and they are filled and repeated together as a unit. A group is how a template expresses a small record with several fields — say, an action with its label, its template and who may see it — rather than a single triple. An optional group can be left out as a whole. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A placeholder is a node in the template typed with one of the placeholder classes and given an rdfs:label; that label is what the form shows as the field's name. The common kinds are: nt:LiteralPlaceholder for a short text and nt:LongLiteralPlaceholder for a longer one; nt:UriPlaceholder for a URI to be minted here and nt:ExternalUriPlaceholder for one that already exists elsewhere; nt:TrustyUriPlaceholder for the URI of another nanopublication; nt:AgentPlaceholder for a person or agent; nt:DatePlaceholder for a date whose precision is left to the author; and nt:RestrictedChoicePlaceholder and nt:GuidedChoicePlaceholder for values chosen from a list or looked up. nt:ValuePlaceholder accepts a text or a URI. A placeholder can carry several types at once, for example a URI placeholder that is also an introduced resource, or a lookup field that is also an nt:ExternalUriPlaceholder, so that the form does not offer to mint a new identifier. nt:NewUriPlaceholder marks the opposite case, a field naming something that must not exist yet. A few further, rarely needed types exist for special cases such as automatically escaped URIs. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A field standing for a person, an organisation or a bot should be an nt:AgentPlaceholder rather than a plain URI placeholder. It gives the form agent lookup and selection, and it marks the value as an agent for anything reading the nanopublication later. Where the person filling in the form is the likely value — an author, a presenter — add nt:hasDefaultValue nt:CREATOR, and the field is pre-filled with the logged-in user. Where the agent must already exist — which is nearly always — type the field nt:ExternalUriPlaceholder as well. Otherwise the form offers whatever name is typed as a new identifier minted on the spot, which then refers to nobody. Leave it off only where the form is meant to describe a new agent. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

An nt:GuidedChoicePlaceholder lets the user search for an existing resource and pick it, instead of pasting a URI. Where to search is given by nt:possibleValuesFromApi: the beginning of a lookup URL, to which the form appends what the user types. The usual source is the nanopublication lookup restricted to one type, which finds things introduced by nanopublications, for instance all spaces or all classes. Wikidata's entity search is the usual source for general topics; it cannot be restricted by type, so it suits open subjects better than fields where only one kind of thing makes sense. Several sources may be listed, and their results are offered together. A lookup only suggests: a name that matches nothing is offered as a new identifier, minted on the spot. For a field that refers to something existing — a space, a template, a class — add nt:ExternalUriPlaceholder, and the form no longer offers to mint one. Since Nanodash 5.20 each suggestion shows, under its label, its URI in short form, where it comes from — the space it belongs to, or else the person who published it — and how long ago it was published, newest first. If a lookup cannot be reached, a line under the field says so and offers to try again. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

An nt:RestrictedChoicePlaceholder offers a closed set of values, listed in the template with nt:possibleValue, one per value, or taken from another nanopublication with nt:possibleValuesFrom. A value outside the set is refused. This makes it the right type for a field that selects between a few well-defined options — a view type, a role tier, on or off — rather than for open-ended content. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

nt:hasDatatype on a literal placeholder both constrains the value and changes the field. With xsd:date or xsd:dateTime, the form shows a date picker instead of a text field. For a point in time coarser than a day, the types xsd:gYear, xsd:gYearMonth, xsd:gMonth, xsd:gMonthDay and xsd:gDay are offered as parts to pick, such as a year alone. A fixed datatype suits a field whose precision the template can decide. Where it is the author's to decide — one person knows only the year, another the hour — use nt:DatePlaceholder instead (Nanodash 5.20 and later). It offers year, month, day, time and timezone, and the published value is typed by what was entered: "2026"^^xsd:gYear, "2026-11"^^xsd:gYearMonth, "2026-11-16"^^xsd:date, or a full xsd:dateTime. On this placeholder, nt:hasDatatype lists the precisions accepted instead of fixing one. The datatype is matched exactly. A placeholder with a datatype does not accept a plain, untyped value, so adding a datatype to a field of an existing template makes the older nanopublications, whose values are untyped, no longer fit it. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Three placeholder roles say where a URI comes from and what it stands for. nt:LocalResource marks a resource minted under the new nanopublication's own URI, so the user only types a short name for it. nt:IntroducedResource additionally records the resource in the publication info with npx:introduces: this nanopublication brings the thing into existence, and the thing has an identity of its own that others can refer to. nt:EmbeddedResource records it with npx:embeds instead: the resource is content that belongs to this particular nanopublication. The difference shows when a nanopublication is superseded. An introduced resource keeps the same URI in every later version, so a new version must refer to the original URI rather than mint another; an embedded resource is expected to get a new URI with each version. Either way, the resource must be something each nanopublication supplies itself: a placeholder, a local resource, or a URI containing the ~~ARTIFACTCODE~~ marker. A fixed URI from elsewhere, marked introduced or embedded, would have every nanopublication made from the template claim the same thing, so since Nanodash 5.20 the form reports such a template as faulty and will not publish from it. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A template is referred to by a URI. In older templates that is the URI of the nanopublication itself. Newer ones tell the template apart from each template version: the version is a node inside the nanopublication, marked as embedded and carrying the statements, and nanopublications made from it name that node. Both forms remain valid. A template version names the template it belongs to with dct:isVersionOf: a URI that the first version introduces and every later version keeps. Templates made since late October 2026 call the two …/template and …/templateVersion. Older ones called the version …/template and the template …/templateKind; those URIs stay as they are, and nothing depends on the names. Like any nanopublication, a template version can be superseded, and forms opened on an older version can offer the latest. A version can also name a space with gen:governedBy; once that space maintains the template, the current version is the newest one published by any member of the space, rather than by the holder of one particular key. This lets a community keep a shared template up to date even when its original author is no longer around. Provenance and publication-info templates work the same way: the forms for defining them offer both statements, and Nanodash follows them there too. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash
documents.s: How templates are identified and versioned

documents.t: Besides its statements, a template can declare a few things about itself. nt:hasTag gives the heading under which it is listed. nt:hasNanopubLabelPattern is a pattern like ${title} that names each published nanopublication after one of its fields. nt:hasTargetNanopubType gives one or more types that every nanopublication made from the template is marked with, which is how such nanopublications can later be found as a group. Two settings reach into the other parts of the form: nt:hasDefaultProvenance names the provenance template the form opens with, and nt:hasRequiredPubinfoElement names publication-info templates that are always included, so that a form never lacks a particular piece of metadata. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Some publication-info templates describe metadata that belongs to one nanopublication alone, such as a "derived from" link, a change note, or the creator. When such a nanopublication is later used as the starting point for another, this metadata must not be copied along, or the new nanopublication would claim things that are no longer true. A publication-info template typed nt:TransientTemplate marks its content as exactly that kind: consumed and dropped when the nanopublication is reused, never carried into the new one. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash
documents.s: Metadata that is not carried forward

documents.t: nt:hasPrefix puts a fixed beginning in front of a URI field, so the user only types what comes after it, and nt:hasPrefixLabel gives that beginning a readable name in the form. The prefix may also contain a token standing for wherever the form was opened: ~~SPACE~~ for the current space, and ~~NAMESPACE~~ for the namespace of the current maintained resource. A template using these mints new resources under the space or vocabulary the user is working in, rather than under a namespace fixed when the template was written. If the form is opened without such a context, it shows a picker to choose one. A URI built from a prefix is not unique by construction: filling in the same name twice would make the second nanopublication quietly add to the first one's resource rather than create a new one. Typing the field nt:NewUriPlaceholder as well makes the form check, before publishing, whether any nanopublication already introduces the resulting URI, and refuse if one does (Nanodash 5.16 and later). Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A nanopublication made from templates records them in its publication info: nt:wasCreatedFromTemplate for the assertion template, nt:wasCreatedFromProvenanceTemplate for the provenance one, and nt:wasCreatedFromPubinfoTemplate, one per template, for the publication-info ones. These links are what allow a nanopublication to be reopened in the form it came from, to be superseded, or to serve as the starting point for another one. They are worth including even in a nanopublication written by hand, since without them it can be read but not maintained through the forms. Each link must name a template of its own kind: a provenance template in the provenance link, publication-info templates in the publication-info links. The usual mistake is naming one of the templates that define provenance or publication-info templates. Since Nanodash 5.22.3 such a link is passed over, and a form opened on the nanopublication falls back to the generic templates. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash
documents.s: How a nanopublication records its templates

documents.t: A form can be opened on an existing nanopublication instead of empty, and the way it is opened decides what the new nanopublication is in relation to the old one. Use copies the content as a starting point for something new and independent; partial does the same but quietly drops whatever does not fit the chosen template. Supersede makes a new version of the same thing: it links back with npx:supersedes and keeps the identifiers of what the old nanopublication introduced. Derive makes a different thing based on the old one, linking back with prov:wasDerivedFrom but minting fresh identifiers. Override links back the same way but keeps the identifiers, which amounts to editing the thing in place — and, unlike supersede, it does not require the same signing key, so it is how someone revises what another person published. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash
documents.s: Starting a form from an existing nanopublication

documents.t: A form can be reached directly by URL, with the template and any number of fields already filled in: /publish?template=<template URI>&param_title=Some+title&param_space=<space URI> Each param_ is followed by the placeholder's short name. Adding template-version=latest opens the newest version of the template instead of the one named. This is how the action buttons on views open pre-filled forms, and it is a convenient way to send someone a ready-to-publish link. How a nanopublication's types and label are found, why they matter, and when to state them explicitly.

Every nanopublication is filed under one or more types, and the types decide where it is found: which repository it lands in, which listings include it, which views show it, whether a lookup for "all spaces" or "all presentations" returns it. A nanopublication with no useful type is stored but effectively invisible. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Types are read off the nanopublication itself, so nothing needs registering. A type stated on the nanopublication in its publication info counts, whether as a plain type or with npx:hasNanopubType. So does every type of a thing the nanopublication introduces, describes or embeds, and every type of its assertion. Two shortcuts cover simple assertions: if all statements have the same subject, that subject's types count, and if all use the same predicate, that predicate itself becomes the type — which is why a one-statement nanopublication saying "X is relevant for Y" is filed under "is relevant for". Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Forms add a type when their template declares one, and most nanopublications get theirs from what they introduce. A nanopublication written by hand, or one whose type cannot be inferred, should state it explicitly with npx:hasNanopubType; otherwise it will not reach the repository where the queries for its kind look. A nanopublication may carry several types, and a query for any of them finds it. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A type's repository is created when the first nanopublication of that type appears, so queries for a brand-new type find nothing until then. When introducing a new kind of nanopublication, publish an example first, marked npx:ExampleNanopub and labelled as such, so that the repository exists and the queries can be tested. Listings leave example nanopublications out. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A nanopublication is shown by its label wherever it is listed, so give it one. The label is taken, in order, from a label on the nanopublication itself, a title on it, a label or title on its assertion, and finally the label of the thing it introduces — so a nanopublication that introduces a labelled term needs no label of its own. Templates can name the nanopublication after one of its fields. A missing label leaves the nanopublication listed by its address, which nobody can read. How a nanopublication is replaced or withdrawn, why only the same key counts, and how deriving and overriding let others build on or revise it.

A nanopublication cannot be changed after it is published: its address is computed from its content, and copies of it sit on several servers. So correcting a mistake, updating a definition, or withdrawing a claim is done by publishing another nanopublication that refers to the first one. The original stays on the network, but every tool learns to treat it as outdated. There are two such moves: publishing a new version, which replaces the old one, and retracting, which withdraws it without replacement. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A new version is a complete nanopublication of its own that names the one it replaces in its publication info with npx:supersedes. Tools then show the new one wherever the old one used to appear, and mark the old one as superseded. Versions form a chain: the newest one supersedes the previous, which superseded the one before. Any address in the chain can be resolved to the current version, so a link to an old version keeps working and leads to the latest state. Nanodash offers "supersede" on any nanopublication, which opens the form pre-filled with its content. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A retraction is a small nanopublication whose assertion says, with npx:retracts, that a given nanopublication is withdrawn. The retracted one remains on the network and can still be opened, but it disappears from listings and search results, and anything it introduced no longer counts. Retracting is the right move for something published by mistake or found to be wrong with nothing to put in its place. If there is something to put in its place, publish a new version instead; that both withdraws the old one and provides the replacement. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

In principle anyone could publish a nanopublication claiming to supersede or retract another, so tools apply one rule: a new version or a retraction is honoured only if it is signed with the same key as the nanopublication it refers to. Otherwise it is stored like any other nanopublication but has no effect on the original. The command-line client will not even build a retraction under a different key. Two consequences follow. A nanopublication signed with a key that is lost can no longer be superseded or retracted by that route. And you cannot revise someone else's nanopublication this way, however wrong it is — for that, see deriving and overriding below. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Many nanopublications introduce something — a term, a role, a view — and give it a URI minted under the nanopublication's own address, recorded with npx:introduces. When such a nanopublication is superseded, the new version must keep that URI exactly, rather than mint a new one under its own address, so that everything referring to the thing keeps pointing at it. The form does this automatically when opened in supersede mode. When writing a new version by hand, this is the one thing to get right: copy the introduced URI from the original, do not let it be regenerated. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash
documents.s: What is introduced keeps its identity

documents.t: Sometimes the aim is not to replace a nanopublication but to make a different one that builds on it: a variant of a definition, an adaptation of a template, a claim narrowed to another case. This is a derivation. The new nanopublication records prov:wasDerivedFrom pointing to the old one, mints fresh identifiers for what it introduces, and leaves the old nanopublication as it is. Since nothing is replaced, deriving works across keys: anyone may derive from anyone's nanopublication. Nanodash offers "derive" next to "supersede". Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash
documents.s: Deriving: a new thing based on an old one

documents.t: An override sits between the two. Like a derivation it records prov:wasDerivedFrom and can be published with a different key; like a new version it keeps the identifiers of what the original introduced. The result is an in-place revision of the same thing by a different person. Whether an override takes effect is not decided by the key but by convention on the page where the thing appears: pages maintained by a community typically show the newest version published by any member of that community. This is how shared content — documentation, vocabularies, views — is kept up to date by a group rather than by whoever happened to publish it first. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

If two people, or one person twice, publish a new version of the same nanopublication independently, the chain forks: two nanopublications both supersede the same original, and tools cannot tell which is current. Pages then tend to keep showing the version they had, or pick one at random. A fork is repaired by publishing one more version that supersedes both heads. To avoid causing one, check what the current version is before superseding, especially for nanopublications that several people maintain. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Tools find the current version by following the chain of npx:supersedes links forward from any version, staying with nanopublications signed by the same key, and stopping at the last one that has not itself been superseded or retracted. Nanopub Query provides this as a service, so every tool resolves versions the same way. For things governed by a space, an alternative rule applies alongside: the current version is the newest one published by a member of that space, whatever key signed it. That is what allows a community to carry a definition forward after its original author has left. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash
documents.s: How the current version is found

documents.t: Before superseding, make sure you are superseding the current version and not an older one. Keep the introduced identifiers. Add a short change note when a new version is more than a typo fix; the form offers a field for it. Retract promptly when something is wrong and there is no replacement, since the retracted nanopublication is otherwise taken at face value. And do not fear the permanence: a superseded or retracted nanopublication is hidden from everyday use, but it remains available to anyone who cites it, which is exactly what citing something should mean. Who you are on the network: your ORCID, your signing key, your introduction, and what approval means for you.

On the nanopublication network a person is identified by their ORCID, the identifier researchers use across publishers and funders. Nanodash logs you in through ORCID, and everything you publish names your ORCID as creator. Your page on Nanodash — reached from your name anywhere — lists your introductions, the spaces you belong to, and what you have published. ORCID says who you are; it does not by itself let you publish. For that you need a signing key, and the network needs to know that the key is yours. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash
documents.s: Who you are on the network

documents.t: Every nanopublication is signed, so you need a key pair. Nanodash makes one for you on your profile page and keeps it with your account, so you can publish from any browser after logging in. If you also publish from the command line, that tool keeps its own key in a file on your computer. The private half of a key never leaves the place it was made. The public half is published, in your introduction, so that anyone can check your signatures. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

An introduction is a nanopublication that links a key to you: it names you, states your public key, and is signed with that very key. Nanodash creates and publishes it from your profile page when you make a key. It is the one nanopublication everything else depends on, since it is how the network learns which signatures are yours. Each key gets its own introduction. A person with a key in Nanodash and another on their laptop has two introductions, and both keys count as them once approved. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A freshly introduced key is not trusted yet. Someone whom the network already trusts has to approve your introduction, by publishing a short nanopublication saying so — typically a colleague, a space admin, or whoever invited you. Nanodash offers this to them where your introduction is shown. Until then you are pending: you can publish, and your nanopublications are stored, but wherever the network asks "who published this?" the answer is not yet you. Roles granted to you show up but do not take effect, and content restricted to members of a space does not include yours. Two things count already: declaring yourself an observer of a space, and choosing the views on your own page. Approval takes effect on the next completed trust round, which is a matter of minutes, occasionally longer. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A key in Nanodash stays with your account for as long as the instance exists. A command-line key is a file on your computer, and if that file is lost nobody can recover it. Nothing signed with a lost key can be superseded or retracted any more — those nanopublications stay as they are, and their content can only be replaced by new nanopublications made with a new key, which others will see as separate publications. So keep a backup of a command-line key, and treat any key like a password: do not share it, and if it may have leaked, make a new one and stop using the old. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

It is normal to have more than one key: one in Nanodash, one on each machine you script from, one for a bot you run. Each has its own introduction and its own approval, and all of them are yours. Roles in spaces are granted to you, not to a key, so they apply whichever key you sign with — as long as that key is approved. Bots are the exception: a bot is its own agent with its own identity and roles, owned by you rather than being you. Bundles of views and roles assigned to a resource: assigning, versions, and how presets and displays combine.

A preset is a named bundle of views and roles for a kind of page: "the layout for a project space", "what an event page needs". Assigning a preset to a space or resource attaches all of its views at once, and makes its roles available there, instead of one display and one role attachment at a time. A preset is defined once and assigned to as many pages as fit it. A preset names the page types it is meant for, its views — some marked as top-level, shown even where the page has no other content — and its roles. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A preset is assigned to one resource by a nanopublication that names the preset and the resource; admins and maintainers do this for a space and its resources. It is removed by a later nanopublication naming the same pair as deactivated, whoever published the first. The newest wins. What identifies an assignment is the preset together with the resource, not the particular preset version it names. Assigning a newer version of the same preset therefore replaces the earlier assignment rather than adding a second one. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A preset has versions the way a view has: the preset stays the same, and each preset version names it with dct:isVersionOf. Assignments do not follow new versions on their own: an assignment pins the preset version it named, and moving to a newer one is a deliberate act — the About tab of a page shows when a newer version of an assigned preset exists, published by the same person as the assigned one, and offers to update. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Views brought by a preset and views attached by individual displays share one pool per page, resolved by time: a display published after the preset assignment can switch off or adjust one of the preset's views for that page, and a preset assigned later can override earlier displays. A preset thus gives a page its baseline, and displays fine-tune it. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash This page is a copy of the topic Preset of the Nanopublication Docs. Nanopublications that stay on a local registry and never reach the public network: marking, routing, and expectations.

A protected nanopublication is one that stays on a local, private registry and never reaches the public network. It is meant for organisations that run their own nanopublication infrastructure and want to use it for content that is not for the world: internal records, drafts, data under restriction. In every other respect it is an ordinary nanopublication — signed, immutable, with the same four parts — and it can be read, superseded and retracted within the instance that holds it. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A nanopublication is protected when its publication info types the nanopublication itself as npx:ProtectedNanopub. This has to be a type of the nanopublication, not a "nanopublication type" annotation of the kind used for classifying content: registries check the former and ignore the latter, so a nanopublication that only looks protected would be sent to the public network. Nanodash adds the marker through a checkbox in the publish form, offered only when the instance it runs on is a local one. Where a form is opened on a protected nanopublication, or uses a protected template, the box is ticked and cannot be cleared, so nothing protected can leak through a copy. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A registry accepts protected nanopublications only if it is configured as a local instance, and says so in its status. Publishing tools check this per registry: a protected nanopublication is sent only to registries that report themselves local, and if none is available, publishing fails with a message saying so rather than quietly falling back to the public network. Public query services likewise refuse to load them. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Protected does not mean private within the instance: everyone with access to the local registry can read it, and the organisation running the instance can remove it — unlike on the public network, where nothing is ever removed. Whether new nanopublications are protected by default is a setting of the instance. The public network and the local instance are separate worlds. A protected nanopublication can refer to public ones, but a public nanopublication that refers to a protected one carries a link nobody outside can follow, which is why a form with a protected source keeps the result protected too.
