The repositories a query can run against: full, meta, text, per-type, per-key, spaces and trust, and how to combine them.

Nanopub Query, the service behind every page and API call, does not keep all nanopublications in one database. It keeps several repositories, each holding a slice of the network suited to a kind of question, and a query template names the one it runs against. Choosing the right repository is the difference between a query that answers in a moment and one that times out. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

full holds every nanopublication with all its content; it answers anything, but slowly for broad questions. meta holds only the information about each nanopublication — who published it, when, what it supersedes or introduces — and is the fast choice for questions that do not need the content. text supports full-text search over the content, and last30d holds only recent nanopublications, for feeds and dashboards. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

For each nanopublication type there is a repository holding only nanopublications of that type, and for each publisher's key one holding only theirs. A query about, say, presentations runs against the presentations repository and never touches the rest, which is what makes views fast. A type's repository comes into existence when the first nanopublication of that type is published — until then, a query naming it finds nothing — so a new kind of nanopublication is introduced with an example first. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash
documents.s: Repositories by type and by publisher

documents.t: Two repositories hold state the service computes rather than nanopublications as published. spaces holds the validated picture of every space — its members and their roles, its resources, its sub-spaces — with the authority checks already applied. trust holds which keys belong to whom and whether the network trusts them. Queries about "who may" and "who is" go here rather than reconstructing the answer from raw grants and introductions. Both keep the current state in a graph whose name changes on every recomputation, reached through a pointer; a query reads the pointer and the state in one go so it never sees a half-updated picture. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A query on one repository can consult another with a federated service clause, typically to filter content by space membership: fetch the members from spaces, then keep only the rows whose publisher is among them. Such a clause is best written as a self-contained sub-query sharing no variables with the rest, so it runs once rather than once per row. In a query template the repository is named with the generic address https://w3id.org/np/l/nanopub-query-1.1/repo/…, which resolves to whichever instance answers, never with the name of one server. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Every query template is also an API: https://query.knowledgepixels.com/api/<artifact code>/<query name>?resource=… runs it with the given parameters. The format of the answer follows the request's Accept header. A browser gets XML, which most show as an empty page, so add .csv or .json to the query name to see the rows there. Each repository also has a SPARQL editor of its own, linked from the repository's page on the service. Scripts and bots are better served by https://router.knowledgepixels.com/query/…, which forwards each request to a query instance that is currently healthy. Two calls may then reach different instances, so a nanopublication published a moment ago can be visible to one and not yet to the next. The test network has a query service of its own, https://test.query.knowledgepixels.com/, which sees only what was published there. Views that make up the pages of spaces, people and resources: kinds, queries, placement, versions, and making one.

A view is a block on a page — a table, a list, a text, a diagram — filled from a query over the network. The pages of spaces, people and maintained resources are made almost entirely of views: the member list, the messages, the vocabulary's classes, this documentation's paragraphs are each one view showing the results of one query for the page's resource. A view is a nanopublication. It names the query, says how to show the results, which kinds of page it belongs on, where on the page it goes, and which buttons it offers. Defining a new view needs no programming: a query plus a view nanopublication is a new kind of page section. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

The view type decides how rows are shown. A tabular view is a table with one column per result variable. A list shows one linked item per row, run together on a line; an item list shows them one below the other. A plain paragraph view shows each row as a heading and a block of text. A nanopublication set view shows each row's nanopublication in full, and none of the other columns. An SVG view shows one diagram per row, drawn by the query itself, and a network view draws each row as a link between two nodes, in a diagram that can be rearranged and clicked through (Nanodash 5.20 and later). A header view has no query and no rows: it is just a section heading with optional actions. Separately from its type, a view can be made a query form: the page then shows a form for those query parameters that the page does not fill itself, and the results open on a page of their own, laid out according to the view's type. Every view keeps the type gen:ResourceView alongside its specific one; that is the type everything else looks for. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A view names a published query template and the parameter it fills with the page's resource, usually resource. When the page opens, the query runs with that value, and the rows become the view's content. Result columns holding a URI are shown as links, with a companion label column giving the link text; a np column at the end links each row to its source nanopublication. The same query can back several views, and a view can be re-pointed at a newer query by publishing a new version of the view. Query references are exact, so improving a query means updating the views that use it. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A view declares which kinds of page it is for: spaces, people, maintained resources — any combination. A view for the pages of parts of a resource, such as the terms of a vocabulary or the paragraphs of a documentation, instead names the class of those parts, or the namespace their URIs fall under. Declaring where a view belongs does not put it on any page yet. That is done by a display, which attaches a view to one particular resource, or by a preset, which attaches a bundle of views to every resource of a type. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Views are laid out in sections down the page, and within a section from left to right. A view's position is a short code such as 4.2.members: the first digit is the section, the second orders views within it, and the rest is a name for readability. Sections 3 to 7 are in use, from an introduction section at the top to a closing one at the bottom; the default is 5.5.default. A view may take the full width or a fraction of it, given in twelfths, so two half-width views sit side by side. Long results are paged; the page size is the view's to set. A display can override all three for one resource. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A view and its versions are two different things. The view is a URI that stays the same across versions; each view version names it with dct:isVersionOf and holds the query, the type and the actions. Views made since late October 2026 call the two …/my-view and …/viewVersion; older ones call the view …/my-view-kind and the version …/my-view, which works just as well. A display or a preset names a view version — the node its view nanopublication embeds — and Nanodash moves on from there to the newest version. Naming the view itself instead does not work: the view simply does not appear. A view can additionally be governed by a space that lists it as a maintained resource; then the newest version published by any member of that space is current, so a community can keep its shared views up to date without depending on one person's key. Two people publishing a new version of the same ungoverned view independently produce a fork, which pages resolve by keeping the version they had. It is repaired by one version superseding both. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A view is made with the "Declaring a resource view" form: pick the type, the query and its parameter, the page types, a title with a leading emoji as its icon, a position, and any actions. Test the query first with the page's resource as the parameter, since a view is only as good as its query. The form also takes an optional description, shown under the view's title wherever it is displayed. Most views need none, since the title and column headings already say what they show; keep it for a view whose purpose is not evident, and then to one line. The result appears in the list of views, from where a space admin can attach it to a page. A view nobody has attached is harmless: it exists, and does nothing until displayed. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash This page is a copy of the topic Resource view of the Nanopublication Docs. Each paragraph is a nanopublication. In Nanodash you also find their examples, related paragraphs, and version history, and members of the nanopub space can edit them there.
Bots and tools that publish under their own identity: keys, introductions, approval, joining a space, publishing as the agent.

A software agent is a program that publishes nanopublications under an identity of its own, rather than under the identity of the person running it. A bot is an agent that acts autonomously, such as one that imports records from a database or maintains a set of documents; a tool is one that publishes on a person's behalf when asked. An agent can additionally be marked as driven by generative AI. An agent always has an owner, a person who is responsible for what it publishes. Everything the agent signs traces back to that person through its introduction. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

An agent signs with a key pair of its own, separate from its owner's. This is what lets the network tell the agent's nanopublications from the owner's, and it means the agent's key can be retired or replaced without touching anything the owner published. The private key must be kept safe and must never be lost: without it, the agent's nanopublications can no longer be superseded or retracted by the agent, and the agent cannot publish anything further. The public key is published openly, in the agent's introduction. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

An agent comes into existence through an introduction nanopublication, made with the "Introducing a software agent" form. It gives the agent a name and a type, names the owner, and declares the agent's public key. The agent's identity is a URI minted in this very nanopublication. The introduction is signed with the agent's own key, and the agent is recorded as its creator, so the nanopublication is signed by the agent it introduces. The owner appears as the person the assertion is attributed to. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A new key is not trusted by the network on its own. Someone whose key is already trusted has to approve the introduction, by publishing a nanopublication saying so. Until then the agent is pending: its introduction is visible, but nothing it publishes counts anywhere that checks who published what. Approval takes effect when the network next recomputes its trust state, which is done in rounds. The wait is however long is left of the current round — minutes, sometimes longer — and it cannot be hurried from outside. Watching for the agent's key to appear in the trust state is the reliable way to know it is done. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

To have an agent's nanopublications appear in a space — in its listings, its vocabularies, its documentation — the agent is granted a role in that space like any person, by someone entitled to grant it. A general-purpose "helper" role, at member tier, is the usual choice for a bot. The grant can be published right after the introduction; it simply waits, visible but ineffective, until the approval has taken effect. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

The agent's nanopublications are signed with the agent's key and name the agent as the signer and creator. The provenance says where the content comes from — often the owner, or a source the agent processed. Because they are signed with the agent's key, only the agent can supersede or retract them; the owner's key does not count for that. The introduction itself can be revised the same way, for instance to rename the agent, and it can be retracted with the agent's key, which retires the agent. In Nanodash you also find their examples, related paragraphs, and version history, and members of the nanopub space can edit them there.
Collaborative units on the network: creating a space, its admins and roles, sub-spaces, maintained resources, and what its page shows.

A space is a collaborative unit: a group, a project, an organisation, an event, a community. It has a page of its own, a set of people with roles in it, and things it maintains — vocabularies, documentation, collections. Most of what happens on Nanodash happens inside some space. A space is defined by a nanopublication, like everything else, and so is every membership, role and resource attached to it. What you see on a space page is the sum of those nanopublications, filtered by who was entitled to publish each of them. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A space is created with the "Defining a space" form. It asks for a name and a description, the kind of space — alliance, community, division, group, organization, outlet or program — and at least one admin. The space gets an address under https://w3id.org/spaces/, chosen when it is created, and that address is its permanent identity even when the definition is later revised. The nanopublication that first defines a space is called its root definition. The admins it names are the space's founders, and everything else about the space traces its authority back to them. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Admins own a space. They can revise its definition, attach roles to it, grant any role to anyone, declare what the space maintains, and decide what appears on its page. The admins named in the root definition are trusted by construction; a further admin can be added later, but only by an existing admin. The founding admins cannot be removed, not even by themselves, so a space can never end up with nobody in charge. An admin added later can be removed by another admin, or step down. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Everyone else in a space holds a role. Roles come in three tiers below admin: maintainer, member and observer. The tiers form a ladder — each may grant roles below its own. An admin may grant any role, a maintainer may grant member and observer roles, a member may grant observer roles. Observer is the one role people may take for themselves, by declaring their interest in a space. Which roles exist in a space is up to its admins, who attach role definitions such as "team member" or "helper" to it. A role definition says which tier it belongs to and which statement expresses the grant. Granting is then a single nanopublication: this space has this person in this role. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A grant counts only if the person who published it was entitled to. The network checks this against the signing key: the key must belong to someone who, at that moment, holds a high enough role in the space. Grants that fail this test are stored but ignored — the space page does not show them, and the person does not get the access that goes with the role. A newcomer's key is not trusted immediately. Until their introduction has been approved by someone already trusted, they appear as pending: their role is visible, but nothing they publish is yet counted, and content gated to members of the space does not include theirs. Approval takes effect when the network next recomputes its trust state, which can be a matter of minutes or longer. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A role is taken away by publishing a revocation: a nanopublication naming the space, the person and the role. Anyone may revoke a role held by someone below their own tier, and anyone may revoke their own. Revoking does not undo the original grant nanopublication; it overrides it, and a later grant restores the role again. The founding admins are the exception: their role cannot be revoked at all. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A space can be part of another: a working group within a project, a project within an organisation. This is declared with gen:isSubSpaceOf, either in the space's own definition or as a separate nanopublication. The link counts only when an admin of each space stands behind it — one person who is admin of both, or a declaration from each side — so no space can attach itself to another uninvited. Sub-spaces are shown on the parent's page and the parent on the sub-space's page, but membership does not flow between them: being a member of the parent says nothing about the sub-space, and the other way round. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A space can declare that it maintains a resource: a vocabulary, a documentation collection, a dataset, a template. The declaration is made by an admin and gives the resource a page of its own, hosted within the space. A resource may declare a namespace, a URI prefix under which the things belonging to it are minted; such things then get pages as parts of the resource. Membership of the space decides who counts as a maintainer of the resource. Where a resource's content is edited collaboratively — this documentation is an example — it is typically the members of the maintaining space whose contributions are shown. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A space page is made up of views: lists, tables and texts, each backed by a query over the network. Some views come with every space. Others are attached by the space's admins or maintainers, either one by one or as a preset, a bundle of views and roles that gives a space a ready-made layout. Attaching and removing views is itself done through nanopublications, and the newest decision wins. Many views offer actions — a button to add a member, post a message, propose a term. Which actions a visitor sees depends on the role they hold in the space. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash
documents.s: What appears on a space page

documents.t: A space can take charge of a shared definition — a template, a view — so that any of its members may publish the next version, rather than only the person who published the last one. Each version names the space with gen:governedBy, and an admin lists the template or view as a maintained resource of the space. From then on the current version is the newest one published by a member of the space. A governed version whose template or view the space does not maintain yet appears on the space's About tab marked "not listed yet", with an action to list it. This is how a community keeps its shared tools current over time, without depending on any one person's signing key. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A space is usually found by following links: every person's page shows the spaces they belong to, every space page shows its sub-spaces and the resources it maintains, and every resource page names the space that maintains it. The Nanopub Query service also publishes a plain list of all spaces known to the network, for software and for anyone who wants an overview. In Nanodash you also find their examples, related paragraphs, and version history, and members of the nanopub space can edit them there.
Roles in a space: tiers, defining and attaching roles, granting and revoking them, and what a role gives its holder.

A role is a named position that a person or agent can hold in a space: team member, helper, organizer, project lead. Every role belongs to one of three tiers below admin — maintainer, member or observer — and the tier is what decides what the holder may do. The name is what people see; the tier is what the system uses. Roles are defined once, as nanopublications, and can then be attached to any number of spaces. The same "helper" role, say, serves many spaces without being redefined. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A role is defined with the "Declaring a space member role" form. It asks for a label, a short name such as "member", a heading such as "Members" under which holders are listed, and the tier — maintainer, member or observer, with observer as the default. The definition also fixes how a grant is written: the statement that says someone holds the role, either from the person to the space ("Alice is a member of X") or from the space to the person ("X has member Alice"). Optionally it names a template for making grants, which is what puts an "add …" button on space pages. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A defined role does nothing until a space adopts it. An admin attaches it with a single statement, gen:hasRole, and from then on it can be granted in that space and appears in the space's role listings. Roles can also arrive bundled in a preset, together with the views a space uses. An admin can detach a role again with gen:detachedRole. The newer of the two statements wins, and detaching removes the role's availability along with every grant that depended on it. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash
documents.s: Attaching a role to a space

documents.t: Granting is one nanopublication with one statement, in the form the role definition prescribes. On a space page it is done with the role's "add …" action; the form asks only for the person. Who may grant follows the tiers: an admin may grant any role, a maintainer may grant member and observer roles, a member may grant observer roles. Observer is the one role people may take for themselves, by publishing the grant about themselves — which is how someone declares interest in a space before anyone has invited them. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

The statement a role uses to express a grant can be any property, including one from another vocabulary. The network then needs to know which side of the statement is the space and which the person, and it only knows that for a fixed set of common properties. For any other, a grant must carry that information itself, or it is silently ignored — it never reaches the space page, and nothing reports why. A role's assignment template takes care of this: it records the direction in the template, and every grant made through it carries the note along. Grants written by hand need to include it explicitly. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A grant is honoured only if the person who published it held a high enough tier in that space at the time, judged by the key that signed it. Grants failing this test are kept on the network but have no effect. The rule is what makes a role listing trustworthy: nobody can list themselves as a maintainer. A person whose key is not yet approved by the network is shown as pending. Their grant is visible, but nothing they publish is counted until approval takes effect — except declaring themselves an observer, which counts straight away. Approval takes effect when the network next recomputes its trust state — minutes, sometimes longer. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A role is taken away with a revocation: a nanopublication naming the space, the person and the exact role. Anyone may revoke a role held by someone of a lower tier than their own, and anyone may revoke their own role at any tier. Admin roles are the exception — only another admin can revoke one, apart from stepping down — and the admins named in the space's founding definition cannot be revoked at all. Revocations and grants are ordered by time, so a grant published after a revocation restores the role. Nothing is deleted: the history of who held what, and when, remains readable. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Three things follow from a role. The holder sees the actions that are open to their tier on the space's pages — a button visible to members is hidden from observers. Content gated to the space's members includes what they publish: their paragraphs in shared documentation, their terms in a vocabulary. And they may in turn grant roles below their own tier. Admins and maintainers can additionally attach views and presets to the space's pages and declare what the space maintains. An observer holds none of these; the role is a declaration of interest, not a permission. In Nanodash you also find their examples, related paragraphs, and version history, and members of the nanopub space can edit them there.

documents.t: How the network decides whose keys count: seeds, approvals, rounds, and what being pending or skipped means.

Anyone can publish a nanopublication, and anyone can publish one claiming to be somebody. A signature proves that a nanopublication was made with a particular key, but not whose key that is. The network therefore keeps a trust state: the set of keys it accepts as belonging to the people and agents they claim to belong to. Everything that depends on "who published this" — space membership, roles, retractions, member-only content — is answered from that state. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Trust starts from a small set of seed agents named in the network's settings and grows by approval. When a trusted person approves someone's introduction, the introduced key becomes trusted too, and can in turn approve others. A key is accepted when there is a chain of approvals leading back to a seed, up to ten steps long. An approval is itself a nanopublication: the approver states, with npx:approvesOf, the address of the introduction they vouch for. Nanodash offers it as an action where an unapproved introduction is shown. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Approving an introduction says one thing: this key really belongs to the person or agent it names. It is not an endorsement of what they will publish, and it does not make the approver responsible for their content. So approve when you know the person, or have good reason to believe the identity — a colleague, a collaborator, someone invited to your space — and not merely because they asked. For a bot, approving means you believe the named owner really runs it, and that the owner takes responsibility for what it publishes. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

The trust state is recomputed in rounds by the registries. A round starts ten minutes after the previous one finishes, or sooner when new approvals or introductions arrive, and follows approval chains outward from the seeds. Nothing takes effect while a round is running: a key approved during one becomes trusted at the end of the next round that sees the approval. That is why a newly approved person or bot stays pending for a few minutes, sometimes longer, however quickly the approval was published. The registries publish a counter and a timestamp of their trust state, which is the reliable way to tell whether a round has passed. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A key that has an introduction but no chain of approvals yet is pending. Its nanopublications are stored and readable, but they do not count where the publisher matters: the person's roles in spaces show but do not take effect, and their contributions do not appear in content restricted to members. The exceptions are what a newcomer needs to get started: declaring themselves an observer of a space, and choosing the views on their own page. A key that the round has examined and found no path for is marked as skipped. The difference is only in time: an approval published later moves it into the trusted set on a following round. Nothing is ever permanently rejected. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Trust is about identity, not about content. Whether a nanopublication is correct, useful or appropriate is not something the network judges; that is left to the spaces and the people who curate them, through roles, approvals of terms, and the choice of what to show on a page. Nor does trust govern retraction and versioning: those are decided per key, by whether the new nanopublication is signed with the same key as the old one. A trusted person still cannot retract another trusted person's nanopublication. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash This page is a copy of the topic Trust and approval of the Nanopublication Docs. Each paragraph is a nanopublication. In Nanodash you also find their examples, related paragraphs, and version history, and members of the nanopub space can edit them there.
Buttons on views that open pre-filled forms: result and entry actions, visibility, mappings, fill modes and fill queries.

An action is a button on a view that opens a publish form, pre-filled from where it was clicked. "Add member…" on a member list, "edit…" on a paragraph, "approve" on a pending term are all actions. An action names the template to open, which field of that template receives the page's resource, and who may see the button. Actions are what make a page editable rather than merely readable: every change a visitor can make from a page goes through one, and each results in a new nanopublication. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A result action belongs to the view as a whole and sits in its header: "add paragraph…", "ask a question…". An entry action belongs to each row and sits in the row's menu: "edit…", "retract", "approve". A view can have any number of each. A header view, having no rows, can carry result actions only, which makes it a way to give a section of a page a heading with buttons. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

Each action says which visitors see it: everyone, or holders of a role tier in the page's space — admin, maintainer, member or observer, each including the tiers above it — or holders of one specific role. On a person's own page, the person counts as admin. This decides only what is offered. Whether a published nanopublication takes effect is judged separately, by the roles its signer actually holds, so hiding a button is a convenience for visitors rather than a lock. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

An entry action can carry values from its row into the form, by mapping result columns to template fields: the row's term URI into a "term" field, its title into a "title" field. A mapping can also lock the field it fills, for values the action decides rather than proposes. Columns used this way are hidden from the table, so a column that should stay visible is duplicated in the query under a second name for the mapping. A row's button disappears when a mapped value the template requires is empty for that row — which is how a query hides "retract" on rows the visitor did not publish, by leaving the value blank for everyone else. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash
documents.s: Filling the form from the row

documents.t: Instead of a field, a mapping can name how the form is opened on the row's nanopublication: to supersede it, making a new version; to derive from it, making a new thing; or to override it, re-editing the same thing under a different key. The form opens filled with the nanopublication's content. Override is what lets a member correct another member's contribution in place; it works when the row's nanopublication is the one that introduced the thing being edited. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A result action can carry its own small query, run against the page's resource when the form opens, whose first row pre-fills fields: a new presentation's date from the event's date, a question's context from the space's description. The values are defaults, not locks, unless the mapping locks them. Because the query, not the visitor, decides what is suggested, it should read only from sources the page's community controls — the resource's own current definition, its space's members — and never from anything anyone on the network could have published about the resource. In Nanodash you also find their examples, related paragraphs, and version history, and members of the nanopub space can edit them there.

documents.t: Attaching a view to a page, turning it off, adjusting it for one page, and views for the parts of a resource.

A view display attaches one view to one page: this view, on the page of this space, resource or person. It is a small nanopublication, made with "Displaying a view for a resource", and it is what turns a view that exists into a view that shows. Admins and maintainers of a space publish displays for the space and its resources; a person publishes them for their own page. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash
documents.s: Putting a view on a page

documents.t: A display is either activated or deactivated. To remove a view from a page, publish a new display for the same view and page marked deactivated; the newer display wins. This works whoever published the earlier one, since the rule is by time, not by key. Publishing an activated display later turns the view back on. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A display may override the view's own settings for its page: the position, the width, the page size, the title, and the description shown under it. The view keeps its defaults everywhere else. This is how the same view can be a full-width section on one page and a narrow side panel on another. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash
documents.s: Adjusting a view for one page

documents.t: A view meant for the pages of a resource's parts — its terms, its paragraphs, its entries — is displayed on the resource, not on any part. The display then applies to every part the view declares itself for, present and future, so adding a new term or chapter needs no new display. A display can instead pin a view to one particular part, for a section that only that part should have. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash
documents.s: Views for the parts of a resource

documents.t: What a page shows is the sum of three things: views built into Nanodash for that page type, views attached by displays, and views brought by presets. Displays and presets draw from one pool: for each view and page, the newest decision — a display, or a preset assignment — is the one in force. So a later display can switch off a view a preset brought, and a later preset can override an earlier display. The page's About tab lists them all, and says which is in effect. In Nanodash you also find their examples, related paragraphs, and version history, and members of the nanopub space can edit them there.

documents.t: Vocabularies as maintained resources: defining terms, approving them, changing them, and releasing versions.

A vocabulary is a set of defined terms — classes, properties, named individuals — that a community maintains together: the kinds of chemical entity a project works with, the concepts of a domain, the categories of a classification. On the network a vocabulary is a maintained resource of a space, typed as an ontology, with a namespace of its own under which its terms are minted. Each term is its own nanopublication, signed by whoever defined it, so a vocabulary is not one document but a growing collection of small, individually attributable definitions. It is the most common kind of maintained resource on the network. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A term is defined with a form for its kind — class, property or individual — from the vocabulary's page. The form asks for a short name, which becomes the last part of the term's URI under the vocabulary's namespace, a label, a definition, and whatever is specific to the kind, such as the classes a new class falls under. The nanopublication records that the term belongs to the vocabulary. A term can refer to terms of other vocabularies, on the network or elsewhere, wherever a relation to an existing concept is what is meant, rather than a new definition. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A term defined by a member of the space is pending until it is approved. Approval comes in two ways: a member of the space publishes an approval of the term's nanopublication, or the term was published by a holder of the space's auto-approved role, which is how bulk imports and bots contribute without a person approving each term. A member can also disapprove a term, which sets it aside. The vocabulary's page shows approved terms in its Classes and Terms lists, and pending ones separately with approve and disapprove actions, so the state of every term is visible and the decisions are recorded as nanopublications. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A term is revised by publishing a new version of its nanopublication, which keeps the term's URI. Anyone with a role in the space can do this, including for terms others defined; the vocabulary shows the newest approved version. Earlier versions remain on the network, and a term that was defined in error is retracted or disapproved rather than deleted. Because the URI never changes, everything that referred to the term — other vocabularies, data, nanopublications elsewhere — keeps pointing at it through every revision. Nanopublication · Open in Nanodash

A vocabulary changes continuously, term by term. When a fixed reference is needed — for a publication, a dataset, a piece of software — the space releases a version: an index listing every approved term at that moment, with a version number and a page of its own that always shows exactly that set, whatever happens to the vocabulary afterwards. Citing a version therefore means citing a specific, unchanging set of definitions, while citing the vocabulary itself means citing whatever is current. These tools let you create, publish, and query nanopublications. The quick start shows the command-line tool and the JavaScript library in action.

Nanodash (code) is a web interface for browsing, searching, and publishing nanopublications, with templates that make it easy to create them without writing RDF. The Knowledge Collaboratory helps annotate biomedical text, publish those annotations as nanopublications, and browse them.

The nanopub-java release jar is also a command-line tool, with commands such as check, sign, publish, retract, query, and mkkeys: java -jar nanopub-<version>-jar-with-dependencies.jar check my-nanopub.trig The jar is on Maven Central, and the quick start shows how to download the latest one.

nanopub-skill is an Agent Skill that lets AI coding agents work with nanopublications in natural language: creating, signing, publishing, querying, superseding, and retracting them, as well as authoring templates, resource views, and Spaces. It follows the open Agent Skills format, and so works with Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and many other agents.

Nanopublications are a rapidly growing technology, fully based on Semantic Web standards and principles. At this tutorial, participants are introduced to the concept and then immediately get hands-on experience in creating and publishing their own nanopublications as well as querying and using the available content. The tutorial covers how to create nanopublications manually via web forms and automatically via software libraries, how to retrieve published nanopublications from the decentralized network, how to craft own web forms via templates, how to query the network with SPARQL, and how trust and communities are handled. Moreover, participants get brief introductions into a selection of existing systems and approaches that are based on this technology. The attendees will get supervision and advice from the core people driving the nanopublication technology, and will have time during the tutorial to make some first concrete steps in applying it to their areas of interest. At the end, attendees will have a comprehensive basic foundation on the theory and practice of nanopublication technology.

The objective of this tutorial is to give attendees the skills needed to work with nanopublications, along with the knowledge on how they may be applied in scientific work. This tutorial will briefly cover the conceptual framework and motivation, and then focus on providing practical hands-on experience on the usage of nanopublications, covering the whole data lifecycle from creating nanopublications to connecting, querying, combining, and reusing them. This was the first nanopublication tutorial of this kind. Its material builds upon numerous presentations, seminar sessions, and publications we have authored on the topic, and is designed to be easy to update and reuse for further editions.

The target audience are Semantic Web researchers and developers, and generally anyone interested in the technical aspects of nanopublications. The learning goals are the following: Participants know the motivation and vision behind nanopublications Participants know the technical basis of nanopublications and how they relate to other semantic technologies Participants can create their own nanopublications, via the Nanodash user interface as well as programmatically Participants know how to publish and query nanopublications Participants know the basics of how to create their own nanopublication templates Participants understand how agents are identified and trusted on the decentralized nanopublication network Participants have made their first steps in using nanopublications for a small project of their choosing

The tutorial day included sessions on the following topics: What are nanopublications? Creating and publishing nanopublications Creating nanopublication templates Querying nanopublications Applications Trust and communities Individual projects The detailed schedule with the materials can be found here.

Tobias Kuhn is Assistant Professor at VU University Amsterdam, and more recently CTO at the start-up Knowledge Pixels. He is one of the main drivers behind the nanopublication technology and community, having published more than 15 peer-reviewed articles on nanopublications and having led the development of nanopublication software such as nanopub-java and Nanodash. He has also extensive experience with tutoring and lecturing, having organized and taught more than 30 courses at university level over the last 20 years on topics including knowledge organization and information retrieval.

Barbara Magagna is the FAIR Development and Fellowship Coordinator at GO FAIR Foundation (GFF) with a background in landscape ecology, GIS and semantics. She is trainer of the 3-Point FAIRification Framework, for which she developed core components. Nanopublications are at the core of GFF’s Capacity Building Programme leveraging the documentation of FAIR Supporting Resources. Within European projects (ENVRI, eLTER, PARC, FAIR2Adapt) she helps to assess FAIRness of data and services and to develop semantic frameworks (I-ADOPT).

Vincent Emonet is a senior researcher at the Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics (SIB), specializing in semantic web technologies, data integration, and scientific knowledge representation. He has extensive experience in teaching and supervision, having co-organized numerous workshops and tutorials around the topics of the FAIR data principles in general and nanopublications in particular. Vincent is dedicated to empowering scientists with practical skills and tools for managing and sharing structured scientific knowledge. His work has led to many scientific papers on the topic and he has made significant contributions to fostering collaboration and reproducibility in the life sciences.

Piotr Sowiński is a PhD student at the Warsaw University of Technology and a co-founder of the start-up NeverBlink. His work revolves around the topics of Knowledge Graphs, streaming, and distributed systems. He is currently leading two community initiatives that use nanopublications: RiverBench (with structured reporting of RDF benchmarks), and the RDF Stream Taxonomy (with a living literature review of RDF streaming). He also contributes to the open source projects powering the nanopublication ecosystem. Since 2022 Piotr has been teaching hands-on classes about Knowledge Graphs for graduate students.
